forces.title: AI-driven maintenance transforms operational efficiency and asset availability
forces.description: The integration of AI and new technologies is fundamentally rewiring maintenance operations across asset-heavy industries. This shift enables predictive, risk-based reliability management, moving away from reactive approaches. AI tools facilitate rapid asset hierarchy updates, FMEA development, and preventive maintenance planning. Examples include reducing asset on ground (AOG) time by 14% for an airline and increasing technician productivity by 85% for a manufacturer. This transformation generates significant cost savings (10-15% of total conversion costs) and improves asset uptime (1-8 percentage points), profoundly altering asset management practices.
forces.source_title: Maintenance meets AI: A proven approach for asset-heavy industries

forces.title: Soaring global electricity demand fuels transformer market supercycle
forces.description: Global electricity demand, projected to increase by 3.1% annually to 38,000 terawatt-hours by 2035, is a primary driver of the transformer supercycle. This surge is largely fueled by increasing electrification across industries and significant data center expansion, which alone accounts for roughly 70% of North America’s and 30% of Europe’s power demand growth. The electrification of road transport and adoption of electric technologies like heat pumps also contribute, directly translating into higher demand for transformers to manage increased power flows and grid investment.
forces.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply

forces.title: Renewables integration drives increased demand for power transformers
forces.description: The global shift towards a renewables-heavy energy mix, with installed capacity projected to reach 70% by 2035, significantly increases transformer demand. Renewables require more transformer capacity per unit of delivered energy because generation is often located far from load centers, assets operate at lower utilization rates (e.g., solar for 2,140 hours/year vs. gas for 5,120 hours/year), and energy sources are more dispersed. This multiplication of grid-connection points, coupled with the need for bidirectional transformers for energy storage, fundamentally restructures demand in the heavy electrical equipment market.
forces.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply

forces.title: Global transformer supply shortage constrains grid expansion and project timelines
forces.description: A severe global supply shortage for transformers, with a backlog exceeding 1,000 GVA in 2024 and projected to reach 1,690 GVA by 2030, presents a critical headwind across the Industrials sector, particularly for EPC contractors and capital goods providers. Manufacturing capacity is concentrated and slow to expand, relying on specialized labor and scarce raw materials. This scarcity extends lead times from one year to five and drives prices up by over 50%. The shortage fundamentally limits new capacity additions for generation, industrial, and data center projects, delaying timelines and raising costs.
forces.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply

forces.title: UK construction output contracts due to confidence, costs, and subdued investment
forces.description: The UK construction sector is experiencing a significant headwind, with output forecast to contract by 3.3% in 2026, a downgrade from earlier projections. This decline is driven by weakening confidence, rising financing and construction costs, worsening project viability, and subdued investment activity. Private housing and repair, maintenance, and improvement (RMI) activities are expected to see the sharpest declines (-10.0% and -8.0% respectively). Elevated insolvency levels across firms of all sizes underscore the financial stress, making robust credit assessment of counterparties and supply chain resilience critical for businesses.

forces.title: High energy and commodity costs squeeze margins in UK manufacturing and machinery
forces.description: UK manufacturers and machinery & equipment businesses face severe headwinds from persistently high energy and raw material costs. Energy costs are constraining growth and investment for almost 9 in 10 manufacturers. Rising aluminum prices and broader commodity volatility add to costs in the machinery sector, where pricing power is limited. This cost inflation, alongside wage pressures, reduces financial flexibility and weighs on profitability. Businesses must prioritize cost and cash management, as well as diversifying supply chains, to mitigate the impact of these elevated input expenses and protect liquidity.

forces.title: Increasing demand from defense and security sectors boosts manufacturing
forces.description: Geopolitical uncertainty is reshaping industrial priorities, leading to growing demand from defense and security customers for UK manufacturers. More than three-quarters (77%) of manufacturing leaders now view working with the defense sector more positively, and 72% report increased demand from these customers. This represents a significant upside driver for the sector, particularly for aerospace & defense and advanced engineering segments. Firms are adapting investment plans to capture opportunities in these strategically important markets, which offer robust order books and public spending support, strengthening revenue visibility despite broader economic challenges.
forces.source_title: Manufacturing: the gears driving Britain’s growth

forces.title: UK aviation faces stringent decarbonization mandates threatening growth
forces.description: The UK aviation sector faces a significant headwind from increasing pressure to decarbonize, with a mandate to abate 100% of emissions by 2050 to align with Net Zero targets. Current policies are insufficient, and Heathrow expansion would compound the problem, increasing whole-economy residual CO2 emissions. This necessitates substantial investment in sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) and engineered removals, likely increasing ticket prices significantly. The industry must develop robust policies, funding, and timelines to meet these targets, otherwise, growth in demand for flying will be constrained, posing a commercial risk for airport operators and airlines.
forces.source_title: Advice to the UK Government on proposed Heathrow Airport expansion

forces.title: Chinese OEMs disrupt European truck market with cost and speed advantages
forces.description: The entry of Chinese OEMs is a profound structural change for the European truck industry. These players leverage a 30-40% structural cost advantage, faster development cycles (22-28 months vs. 40-48 months), and innovative integrated energy solutions. While their current European market share is low, it's rapidly increasing in specific commercial vehicle segments. Chinese OEMs are positioned to achieve double-digit market shares by 2035, challenging the dominance of incumbent European manufacturers. This forces European OEMs to accelerate their ZE technology leadership, enhance cost-competitiveness, and develop new go-to-market models to defend their position.
forces.source_title: Competing against Chinese innovation speed in European trucking

forces.title: Zero-emission truck transition drives need for vast charging infrastructure
forces.description: The transition to zero-emission trucks (ZETs) is a critical structural change in the European trucking industry. While ZEVs offer TCO advantages for 30% of use cases, widespread adoption is hampered by insufficient charging infrastructure. Europe needs 15,000-20,000 public and 200,000 fleet hub charging points by 2030, requiring over €40 billion in investment by 2035. Bottlenecks in grid access and derisking investments for infrastructure operators are key challenges. Overcoming these is crucial to accelerate decarbonization and avoid significant economic costs, making infrastructure development a binding constraint for ZET deployment.
forces.source_title: Competing in the fast lane—the future of Europe’s truck industry

forces.title: Autonomous vehicle technology poised to address driver shortages and create value
forces.description: Autonomous vehicles (AVs), especially in trucking and buses, are emerging as a significant upside driver for the Industrials sector. Autonomous road freight could become a €100 billion value pool by 2035 in Europe, driven by TCO reductions and a shift towards high-margin software and services. Autonomous city buses are expected to capture 60% of their market by 2045, critically addressing severe driver shortages (e.g., 80,000 bus drivers in Germany by 2030). Despite Europe trailing other regions, upcoming regulations will enable scale, transforming vehicle types, service models, and creating new profit streams for OEMs and technology providers.
forces.source_title: Competing in the fast lane—the future of Europe’s truck industry

forces.title: Erosion of brand loyalty in European truck market creates competitive shifts
forces.description: The European truck market is undergoing a structural change characterized by diminishing brand loyalty among fleet operators. The industry's average Net Promoter Score (NPS) has dropped significantly, with one-third of operators likely to switch brands for their next purchase, and another third expressing no strong affiliation with current OEMs. This creates a large pool of undecided buyers and opportunities for new entrants, particularly Chinese manufacturers who are perceived well on price and technology. Incumbent European OEMs must urgently focus on cost competitiveness, customer satisfaction, and leveraging defensible assets like integrated portfolios and strong service networks to counter this erosion.

viewpoints.title: AI transformation offers significant value in asset-heavy industries' maintenance operations
viewpoints.description: McKinsey identifies a significant opportunity for asset-heavy industries, including airlines and rail, to unlock two to five percentage points of incremental margin through end-to-end maintenance transformation using AI. The approach can reduce maintenance costs by 10-15% and increase asset availability by up to eight percentage points. The key is not just technology adoption, but embedding AI solutions into daily workflows for reliability engineers and technicians, enabling data-driven insights and shifting decision-making closer to assets. This improves efficiency in planning, execution, spare parts, and contractor management, reducing downtime and costs.
viewpoints.source_title: Maintenance meets AI: A proven approach for asset-heavy industries

viewpoints.title: Transformer market enters supercycle with demand outstripping supply
viewpoints.description: McKinsey states that the global transformer market is in a supercycle, driven by structural demand increases from electrification, renewable energy integration, and aging grid infrastructure replacements. Supply is constrained by capital-intensive manufacturing, specialized labor, and tight raw material supply. This has turned transformers from a procurement detail into a strategic priority, leading to extended lead times (up to five years) and surging prices (>50% since 2021). The supply deficit is expected to persist into the next decade, impacting grid build-out and renewable capacity additions.
viewpoints.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply

viewpoints.title: UK Construction sector faces contraction, elevated insolvencies, and financial stress
viewpoints.description: Allianz UK reports a weakened outlook for the UK construction sector, forecasting a 3.3% contraction in 2026, worse than previous estimates. This decline is attributed to weakening confidence, rising financing and construction costs, and subdued investment. Insolvency levels remain high, with construction accounting for 17% of all corporate insolvencies in England and Wales. Financial stress is spreading to mid-sized firms, not just SMEs, indicating widespread challenges. Businesses must prioritize assessing counterparty financial strength and supply chain resilience amidst project delays and failures.

viewpoints.title: UK Machinery & Equipment sector hampered by deferred investment and uneven demand
viewpoints.description: Allianz UK indicates a challenging outlook for the UK Machinery & Equipment sector, as companies defer major projects amid economic uncertainty and tight monetary conditions. Uneven global demand fails to offset domestic weakness, while rising commodity prices add to costs without corresponding pricing power. Lenders are becoming more selective due to the sector’s cyclical nature. Businesses with stronger balance sheets and diversified end markets are better positioned, while those highly exposed to specific customers or geographies face greater pressure. Financial flexibility and efficiency-boosting investments are critical.

viewpoints.title: UK Transport sector sees moderate growth but profitability constrained by high costs
viewpoints.description: Allianz UK describes the UK transport sector as experiencing moderate but uneven demand growth, with slight improvements in profitability. However, high costs continue to constrain returns, and liquidity remains fragile amid persistent headwinds. The legal and business environment is supportive but challenging, with regulation and funding constraints shaping performance. Operational improvements have not yet translated into a clear reduction in credit risk. Businesses should focus on tight cash flow and cost control, and assess counterparties by segment due to varied performance.

viewpoints.title: UK Transport Equipment benefits from demand, but profitability and liquidity remain strained
viewpoints.description: Allianz UK highlights that the UK transport equipment sector benefits from strong demand, particularly in aerospace, defense, and selected rail/maritime programs. Robust order books, aftermarket activity, public spending, and export visibility support production. However, profitability and liquidity remain under strain due to rising input costs (oil, transport, metals), unrepaired supply chains, and erratic rolling-stock procurement. Smaller suppliers are more exposed than prime contractors, as benefits are not evenly distributed. Sustained improvement requires stronger financial resilience across the entire supply chain, beyond just demand growth.

viewpoints.title: UK Manufacturing confident despite headwinds, investing in resilience and future growth
viewpoints.description: Barclays UK reports strong confidence among UK manufacturing leaders (94% confident for the next 12 months) despite tough operating conditions, particularly rising energy costs. Investment is increasingly focused on resilience, productivity, and future competitiveness, with 87% noting automation's help in navigating disruption. Manufacturers are prioritizing AI, advanced technologies, and low-carbon innovation. They are also positioning to capitalize on growing demand from defense, security, and critical infrastructure markets, with 77% more positive about defense sector work. Larger firms are investing, while SMEs focus on liquidity.
viewpoints.source_title: Manufacturing: the gears driving Britain’s growth

viewpoints.title: Heathrow expansion risks UK Net Zero target without robust aviation decarbonization policies
viewpoints.description: The Climate Change Committee (CCC) advises that proposed Heathrow expansion is inconsistent with the UK’s 2050 Net Zero target unless the aviation sector fully abates its emissions through policy-driven sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) and engineered removals. Current policies are insufficient, with aviation emissions projected to rise. Expansion would increase whole-economy residual CO2 emissions by 6.9% of expected 2050 levels. The CCC advocates a 'polluter pays' approach to fund decarbonization and manage demand, suggesting ticket price increases. Robust, long-term policy is needed to avoid reliance on other sectors for abatement.
viewpoints.source_title: Advice to the UK Government on proposed Heathrow Airport expansion

viewpoints.title: Chinese truck OEMs pose significant competitive threat to European incumbents
viewpoints.description: McKinsey highlights that Chinese truck OEMs are accelerating their expansion into Europe, leveraging structural cost advantages (30-40% lower even with local EU production), faster R&D cycles (twice as fast), and innovative business models. While currently holding less than 1% of the overall European truck market, their share in specific commercial vehicle segments (e.g., forklifts, electric buses) is rising rapidly. This presents a substantial challenge to established European manufacturers, who need to reassess strategies to defend their market position as Chinese players could capture double-digit market shares by 2035.
viewpoints.source_title: Competing against Chinese innovation speed in European trucking

viewpoints.title: Autonomous truck technology set to transform European road freight and urban mobility
viewpoints.description: McKinsey sees autonomous vehicles (AVs) fundamentally changing road freight and urban mobility in Europe. Autonomous road freight is projected to become a €100 billion value pool by 2035, shifting value from hardware to software and services. Autonomous buses will address driver shortages and enable smaller, more flexible fleets, with 60% market penetration by 2045. While Europe trails the US and China due to regulatory and geographic factors, upcoming UN regulations will pave the way for scale-up post-2030, presenting significant opportunities for industry players to capture new profit pools.
viewpoints.source_title: Competing in the fast lane—the future of Europe’s truck industry

viewpoints.title: European truck fleet operators exhibit diminishing brand loyalty amid rising Chinese competition
viewpoints.description: Bain & Company's 2026 survey reveals a significant drop in European truck operators' Net Promoter Score (NPS) and high willingness to switch brands, with one-third likely to change OEMs. This erosion of loyalty, especially in large and medium fleets, creates an opening for new entrants. Notably, 33% of operators are open to purchasing from Chinese manufacturers, who are perceived favorably on price, TCO, and technology. Western OEMs must urgently address cost competitiveness, customer satisfaction, and articulate strong differentiators to defend market share against agile Chinese rivals.

viewpoints.title: High UK industrial energy prices threaten competitiveness and risk deindustrialisation
viewpoints.description: OEUK highlights that UK industrial energy prices are approximately 75% higher than the G7 average, severely undermining the competitiveness of energy-intensive industries in the UK. This cost disadvantage increases the risk of deindustrialisation and can lead to offshore emissions. Declining domestic energy production exacerbates reliance on imports, making UK manufacturers more vulnerable to international commodity markets and geopolitical risks. The report argues for maintaining affordable, secure domestic energy supplies to underpin the manufacturing base and support strategic industries like defence and aerospace.
